FELICITATIONS TO THE CHAIRMAN 
THE LEADER OF THE HOUSE (DR. MANMOHAN SINGH): Mr. Chairman, Sir, 
I welcome you to this august House with a great sense of joy and pride. I have been a 
Member of this House for over 16 years. So. I say with all sincerity that you come in a 
long line of distinguished Chair persons and you come with great distinction. You have 
had a distinguished service as a diplomat representing our country in important capitals 
of the world and the United Nations. More recently, you have also served the cause if 
education as Vice -Chancellor of the Aligarh Muslim University and the cause of 
impowerment of all our minorities as Chairman of the Minorities Commission. Your 
professional record, your sincere commitment to the ideals and values that define our 
public, your patriotism and your conc ern for the well -being and welfare of our people e 
earned you the respect and admiration of our people. Sir, I am sure, all of this will and 
you in good stead in the years to come as you discharge your onerous responsibility. Sir, 
this House has a unique p osition in our Republic. It is both a House ates and a House of 
Elders. As a House of States, it offers a unique platform for  / region of our country to 
have its voice heard in the highest Councils of Government. House of the Elders, we are 
called upon to reflect with patience and sobriety on ssues of the day and legislations at 
hand. I am sure. Sir, with your wide -ranging rience, you will provide guidance and 
balance to the proceedings of this august se. Sir, I have witnessed the proceedings of 
this House for many years, as itsmber for the past 16 years and as an official of the 
Government of India for almost two decades before that. This House has been witness 
to some very enriching and enlightening debates. However, in recent years, we have 
also witnessed with profound concern and sadness repeated disruptions of proceedings 
and a regrettable unwillingness on occasions to engage in informed dialogue and 
discussion. I hope, Sir, all of this can be put behind us and we can restore to this House 
a sense of dig nity and decorum that is expected of this august House. Sir. I stand here, 
to assure you of the sincere operation of our Government and all constituents of the 
United Progressive Alliance. of us must work together to ensure that this House echoes 
the heartbeat of the n people and lives up to their expectation. Sir, I wish you well and 
wish you the  discharging your onerous constitutional responsibilities. I thank you, Sir.

THE LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): Mr. Chairman, Sir, on my 
personal behalf, on behalf of the party, which I have the honour to represent, and on behalf of 
the office that I hold, constitutionally, as the Leader of the Opposition, I felicitate you on 
the assumption of this office. I greet you for becoming a Member of this Assembly. It is a very 
distinguished club. Very few have the honour of carrying a suffix of just two letters, that is, 
M.P. These two letters are, I believe, letters of great distinction. Please accept our 
collective and my personal congratulations on your election, too, as the Vice-President of the 
country. I have personally advocated that high constitutional offices must remain above 
contention. They ought to be the result of building of consens us, not the outcome of an 
election. But that, nevertheless, is now something that we seldom witness because, perhaps, 
there is a misunderstanding about the true meaning or the import of the word consensus'. 
Consensus is the distillation of consultation. Co nsensus is not merely our abiding by the 
wishes of the majority. And, it is one of the tragedies of the present state of our politics that you 
witness that particular phenomenon more and more on the decline.

occupy, that this Chair is indifferent to political persuasion once the election is over; it is 
indifferent to caste, communities, sects. Here, of course, we don't see that. But in

Party of India, and, I join all the hon. Members of this august House to congratulate you. 
to assure you the fullest cooperation in running this House. Sir, I am new to this 
Parliament, new to this Rajya Sabha so as you are. But, we know you are a great 
academician, a great intellectual, you served as one of the outstanding diplomats, and, 
you have rich experience. Sir, this august House has a glorious tradition and eminent 
persons like Dr. S . Radhakrishnan and Mr. K. R. Narayanan and others served this 
House as Chairmen and served the country as Vice- Presidents, and, now you are the 
Chairman, you are the Vice- President of one of the largest democracies in the world, 
and, we are quite sure that these traditions will be upheld. I must recall the immense 
contribution made by outstanding communist leaders like Shri Bhupesh Gupta who 
served, in this House, for, more than a quarter of century in strengthening the 
parliamentary democracy in our count ry. I think, today, we are at crossroads, and, we 
need to strengthen the parliamentary democracy that we have acquired and we will have 
to strengthen the republican Constitution and the very republic of India. 
Sir, everybody says that Rajya Sabha is the Ho use of Elders but, now. I find that 
there are quite good number of young people also sitting in this House. Rajya Sabha is 
also considered to be House of States and here comes the question of defending the 
federal polity of our nation, the composite cultur e of our nation. There can be 
convergence of interest; there can be conflict of interest. Finally, when we arrive at 
solutions, we should see that the interest of the nation is protected and upheld. That is 
my concern and that should be our approach. 
Sir, this august House should reflect the voice of the weaker sections, the voice of 
the marginalized sections and exploited sections. There are references to the ongoing 
process of liberalisation in the world, the globalisation in the world, but in this proces s, 
the most politically marginalized, economically exploited, socially oppressed people 
should not be neglected and their voice must be heard. I hope, this House will provide 
them an opportunity to be heard, and, listen to their voice and address their con cerns. 
Sir, having said this, I must say that our country is a country which has tremendous 
diversities. In fact, this great nation progresses through these diversities and this country 
remains united through these diversities. And, here there is a need to  uphold the secular 
democracy, the values of secular democracy, and, there should not be any room for 
intolerance, whether it is Treasury Benches, Opposition or the middle path — I do not 
mind — but the country's interest must be protected and upheld. Nobody should 
challenge the secular democratic fabric of our society and the secular democratic 
character of our Constitution, otherwise the country will not be safe. So, Sir, on your 
assumption as Chairman of this august House and Vice -President of our great nation, we 
congratulate you wholeheartedly. We "assure you, having assumed the office of 
Chairman, having assumed the office of the Vice President, we look at you as a great 
Indian, as a great partriot and as a person committed to the country's interest. I  wish you 
all success in your work. And, on behalf of my party, I must make it very clear that you 
can expect fullest cooperation from my party, the Communist Party of India. I wish you 
all success. Thank you.

appreciate you, the most eminent and enlightened bureaucrat. Sir, I have listened to what 
my colleagues have said. In fact, they are not exaggerating. On the other hand, they are 
illustrating what you are. They have seen your background and your experienc e as a 
former IFS officer in various capacities as Ambassador, as High Commissioner, as 
permanent representative in the U.N., as an academician, as a visiting professor, as a 
Vice-Chancellor; and, above all, as a champion of the cause of depressed, oppress ed, 
and suppressed. This is the way I also look at it. 
After seeing your background, I really admire and adore you that this kind of person 
has come to occupy a covetable position like the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Sir, with 
your background, with your e xperience, and with your personality, it may not be very 
difficult for you. Many friends have quoted various couplets. After seeing your 
personality in totality, I am reminded of two famous lines by William Shakespeare when 
he was picturising the most beau tiful woman, Cleopatra, on earth. He said, "Age cannot 
wither her, nor custom stale her infinite variety." Sir, I would put it in masculine gender. 
Age cannot wither you, nor custom stale your infinite variety. You are a person of 
infinite variety. 
Sir, with this background, I want to speak more and more. But paucity of time and 
other constraints warrant me that I should be brief. I shall try to be as brief as possible 
and as quick as possible. 
Before I conclude, I have a word of caution to you. As rightly said by many of our 
colleagues, this is the House of Elders, elders with unique personality, with varied and 
versatile capacity. Every one is unique in his or her own way. Is it so easy to handle 
these people? It. is very difficult. This is the way I would like to caution 
you. 
Secondly, Sir, your predecessor, Mr. Bhairon Singh Shekhawat, was very popular 
and very dynamic. He got absolute understanding with Members in the House. Sir, you 
are succeeding a very popular predecessor. That again, will be a little bit difficult for 
you to equate and excel him. This is my second point. 
My third observation is this. You have to see the Opposition; you have to see the 
right side; and you have to see all the Members. You have to satisfy the entire House. 
While doing so , how you can manage the Treasury Benches, the Opposition Benches 
and the UNPA, are the things you have to consider. As far as I am concerned, what I 
could suggest to you is that when you allocate time, when you give chances, you have to 
be extra considerate with the Opposition, still more considerate with the UNPA and 
more and more considerate with AIADMK which is led by a famous leader, a 
marvellous leader and a mass leader, Madam Jayalalithaa. Thank you, Sir.

DR. BIMAL J ALAN (Nominated): Sir, I too would like to add my voice to felicitate 
you in this Chamber. To welcome you, a lot has been said by more distinguished 
Members about the achievements, the distinction and the contribution that you have 
made to our society. Sir, this House has had some extremely distinguished leaders of 
our society in you position, and I am sure that we are very fortunate in having you too 
in the same position. 
Sir, I do not want to say much because all your qualifications, everything that you 
bring to this House is well -known. But with your permission, I would just  like to add a 
word on one of the issues that has been discussed, which is the role of the Rajya Sabha, 
and this I do from a somewhat different perspective from the one that we have heard 
from some of the distinguished speakers before me. I am a non party person; I am a non-
elected Member, a nominated Member, It also distinguishes us from the independent 
elected Members, that we are non -elected, non -partisan Members. Now. the 
Constitution did provide this. We are here because the Constitution provides that the 
ordinary citizen of India should be represented in some way, in his own capacity, as it 
were, non -elected, i.e. non-political and non -leader. I mean we may have some 
achievements to our credit in some different spheres of our life, but the whole point is 
that we are here. I am here for a very short term unlike all of the distinguished Members 
that you hear who have been here for 15 years, 20 years, 30 years, for seven terms, eight 
terms. I am here for one term. Therefore, I should say one or two words about the role 
of the Rajya Sabha from the perspective of an average citizen, who is here for a short 
time. I share the view of Dr. Alexander that this House has very distinguished body of 
persons from all walks of life, on all sides of the House, irrespect ive of party 
affiliations. So, it is not a point about the individuals or about the quality of the talents 
that we have in this House, but what we have done to the House. That is what I want to 
tell you. 
This House has two or three different characteristic s than the Lok Sabha. First, it 
does not dissolve itself. It is supposed to be the House of States, the Council of States. It 
is supposed to represent the States rather than the parties. It is also supposed to have 
indirect elections. The whole point is th at the legislators of the State Assemblies would 
elect the representatives who can represent that State. Now, what have we done over a 
period of time? It has nothing to do with the individuals; it has nothing to do with the 
parties, but it has something to  do with the way in which you handle this House of 
Elders. You have the anti -defection law. You have the whip. The parties decide who 
will be here. The State legislators nominally vote. But they have no choice. It is open 
voting. You can't defect. There is the whip. So, 

18      Felicitations to [RAJYA SABHA] the Chairman 
depending on you party's strength, depending on your bargaining power, you can elect 
anyone. 
This House is also dominated by parties which was not the original policy. It was 
supposed to be dominated by the representatives of the States, which were elected 
indirectly. It is not happening. I am mentioning this not as a complaint because we are 
very privileged to be here. We don't have the electoral backing for us. All of you are 
leaders, we are individuals. But if you are worried about the separate role of the Rajya 
Sabha, then you have to give some thought to the kind of rules that we have framed, 
over a period of time, through legislation. It is that which is giving a kind of 
undissolving role to this House, which was not envisaged in our Constitution. Maybe, it 
is not necessary. Then, let us say it is not necessary. It is a duplicate of the Lok Sabha 
dominated by parties and that is it. There is no harm in it. You can go through the same 
legislative agenda on which you have neither the "yes'' nor the "no" power. You can 
always pass whatever legislation you want, once it has been passed by the Lok Sabha. 
You can do whatever you want. The executive is supreme. You can dissolve the House 
and re convene after a week. That doesn't matter. But what I am saying is that if you 
want the same thing, let us accept that it is the same thing as the other House. The only 
advantage is that we don't have to dissolve ourselves. The only advantage is that we ca n 
nominate and elect the Members as we wish, and some of us have the great privilege of 
being here and also have the advantage of being here without elections. So, the House 
has its advantages. But it is not a different role. Thank you very much.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Leader of the House, Hon. Leader of the Opposition, Hon. 
Members of the Rajya Sabha, the Indian Parliament, an individual in a multitude of a 
billion  becomes a celebrity when summoned by your sover eign decision to become the 
thirteenth incumbent of this  august office of the Republic. The virtue of the democratic 
process is obvious. Equally evident is the burden of the twin responsibilities  
entrusted. The enormity of the task  induces humility.  I am 

22     Felicitations to [RAJYA SABHA] the Chairman 
overwhelmed by the warmth of your welcome and the confidence you reposed in my 
stewardship of this office. I can hardly find words to express my gratitude. 1 do pledge 
my utmost effort to discharge my du ties with fairness and impartiality and to make 
every effort to protect and defend the rights and privileges of this Council. 
Ours is a parliamentary democracy whose form and objectives are inscribed in the 
Constitution. Its institutions have stood the tes t of time. We, nevertheless, need to 
reiterate and reinvigorate our commitment to them and to their operational modalities. 
In such a system, the majority to my right and the minority to my left, both play an 
equal part. Here, I can do no better than to re call the words in this  House of the first 
Vice-President of India, Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan of revered memory and I quote: 
"A democracy is distinguished by the protection it gives to minorities. A democracy is 
likely to degenerate into tyranny if it do es not allow the opposition groups to criticise 
fairly, freely and frankly the policies of the Government. But, at the same time, 
minorities also have their responsibilities. Well, they have every right to criticise, their 
right to criticise should not deg enerate into wilful hampering and obstruction of the 
work of Parliament. All groups, therefore, have their right and have their 
responsibilities." 
Over the years, this House has developed rules of procedure and conventions for the 
conduct of business. Thes e have been amplified by the rulings of the Chair. They 
constitute an invaluable compendium. The assigned duty of the Chair is to ensure that 
all play by these rules. The referee in a game of hockey or football does carry coloured 
cards in his shirt pocket . A good game, however, is one in which the need to use these 
cards does not arise. It is my fervent hope that with your cooperation, the latter mode 
would characterise our common endeavour. 
Hon. Members, even though I am a new comer to this august body, a s a citizen I am 
not unaware of its deliberations. Much has been done, continues to be done and would 
be done here to promote the national agenda. In an era of rising .expectations, however, 
our work has to respond to changing perceptions and requirements of the people and 
particularly of the weaker sections of our society. They, after all, constitute the 
overwhelming majority of our population. 
The challenge lies in the need to ensure equitable distribution of the fruits of 
development. The challenge also is to seek justice through substantive equity and 
meaningful fraternity. The will to do so is one aspect of it. Institutional efficacy and a 
delivery mechanism is another. Both are integral to the process of change. Delays 
aggravate matters. We need to recall Macaulay's caution: "Excesses of people are 
directed against those whom they suspect of interfering with the public good". Each of 
these imposes an additional responsibility on the representatives of the people. A few 
days back, my very distinguished p redecessor rightly observed, "The quality of 
governance in a democracy will critically hinge on the quality of business transacted in 
the Parliament". 
I make bold to suggest that an awareness of this would be a first step in meeting 
public expectations.

Opening of Kendriya Vidyalayas 
†*21. PROF. RAM DEO BHANDARY : Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Kendriya Vidyalayas in some States are not being opened despite heavy  
demands of the Public as Governments of these States are not making the land and  
buildings available for the purpose as a result of which these schools are being shifted  
to other States; 
(b) if so, the reasons for such negative reaction and mentality of these State  
Governments; 
(c) whether Government are solving thi s issue through administrative pressure and 
dialogue with such States; and 
(d) if so, its present status and the alternative arrangements available with  
Government? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ARJUN SINGH): 
(a) and (b) Kendriya Vidyala yas (KVs) are opened subject to satisfaction of certain 
norms, and subject to the sponsoring authority making available temporary 
accommodation to run the school initially and further making available permanent land 
free of cost to enable Kendriya Vidyalay a Sangathan (KVS) to construct the permanent 
school building. There are some instances of State Governments as sponsoring 
authorities not being able to provide either temporary accommodation or land for 
permanent building, because of which the sanctioned s chools have been shifted to other 
States. 
(c) KVS and the Ministry have repeatedly impressed on the State Governments 
concerned to make available required land and temporary building to open the 
Vidyalayas. 
(d) Out of 50 new KVs sanctioned in August, 2006, 40 KVs are already functional. 
If any State is unable to provide necessary infrastructure despite follow -up, KVS has 
the option to shift the KV to a location where infrastructure is made available. 
Enrolment in Higher Education 
*22. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minsiter of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that his Ministry has targeted to increase the enrolment rate in 
higher education; 
(b) if so, how much intake is likely to be increased and the current intake in all the 
universities; and

(c) whether Government have created adequate infrastructure like laboratories, libraries, 
classrooms, teachers, etc. to achieve the target; and 
(d) if so. the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (d) 
Subject to finalization of the Eleventh Plan, the Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) in higher 
education is proposed to be increased to 15% by 2011-2012, from the present GER of about 10%. 
The existing total enrolment of about 128 lakh students in higher education (2006 -07) is 
proposed to be increased to 212  lakh students by the year 2011-12. 
Public investments are expected to be enhanced during Eleventh Fi ve Year Plan, both for 
establishing new colleges and new universities as well as for strengthening the existing 
institutions. Central Universities, State Universities and Colleges will be supported for creating 
adequate infrastructure in order to address t he concerns of quality, access and equity in higher 
education. 
An important strategy of expansion consists of development of institutional capacity in all 
institutions with special focus on backward, rural, remote areas and small towns. Resources 
permitting, Government is considering to establish 30 new Central Universities and to provide 
some assistance to the State Governments, to incentivise them to establish at least one college in 
each district which has a low GER, during the Eleventh Plan period.

*24. SHRIMATI JAYA BA CHHAN: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a Rajkiya Pratibha Vikas School in Dwarka, in South-West 
Delhi has been awarded ISO -9000 Certificate; if so, the details of efforts made by the 
school for achieving excellence; 
(b) the number of other Government schools possessing this kind of excellence; and  
(c) the steps Government have taken to encourage competitiveness for achieving 
such kind of excellence? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ARJUN SINGH): 
(a) Rajkiya Pratibha Vikas Vidyalaya, Sector -10 Dwarka, New Delhi has been awarded 
IS/ISO 9001:2000 Certificate in June, 2007 for a period of 3 years. The Vidyalaya was 
started on 30th August, 2003. The school had shown excellent results in Centra l Board 
of Secondary Education (CBSE) examinations from the very first batches of classes X 
and XII. The school has excellent infrastructure facilities like well established 
laboratories of Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Geography, Computer Science, General 
Science, Mathematics and Language, music room and Audio Visual rooms. The school 
also has a very good academic track record. 
(b) Rajkiya Pratibha Vikas Vidyalaya, Surajmal Vihar, New Delhi has also been  
awarded IS/ISO 9001:2000 Certificate in June 2007. 
(c) Government of NCT Delhi has encouraged all Rajkiya Pratibha Vikas Vidyalayas 
to apply for such certificates in their quest for excellence. Since a majority of schools  
in the country are under the purview of State Governments, it is for the concerned Stat e 
Governments to encourage competitiveness among its schools to achieve excellence.

Effect of corruption in education 
*26. SHRl SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have received any study report recently from UNESCO's 
Interntational Institute for Educational Planning which reveals that various shades of 
corruption afflict the education system in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and Government's reaction thereto: and 
(c) the details of steps taken or proposed to be taken against such erring institutes in 
the country for securing the career of students? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ARJUN SINGH): 
(a) The Government has seen a Report published in 2007 by UNESCO/International 
Institute of Educational Planning entitled "Corrupt Schools, Corrupt Universities; what 
can be d one?" This report is not India specific and highlights the issue related to 
corruption in education and the consequent loss to the system in terms of its adverse 
effect on access, equity and quality, in developed and developing countries around the 
world. The report includes references to teacher absenteeism and private tuitions by

Statement 
The report presents the conclusions of the research conducted by the HEP in the 
field of ethics and corruption in education. It aims at sensitizing decision -makers, 
educational planners and managers to the importance of combating corruption in 
education; at providing them with key tools to detect and assess corruption problems; 
and at guiding them in the formualtion of adequate strategies to curb malpractices.  
The Report is not I ndia specific. However, references have been made to India 
through out the Report. The points with reference to India are presented below: -  
* In the foreword the Report mentions that ........... Fortunately, as this book amply 
demonstrates, there are vibrant parts of  society — even among the poorest and 
the most vulnerable countries like Bangladesh and India — that will organize in 
support of rational democratic and progressive dismantling of existing corrupt 
practices. 
* Referring to the magnitude of corruption, the Report mentions that there are a 
few estimates of the economic costs of corruption. Two national estimates of  

Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Starred Questions 
corruption corroborate the fact that this is major phenomenon. In India, it was 
estimated at around 20 per cent of the GNP in the 1980s. 
* Decision-makers in Government, academia and advocacy groups have come to 
recognize the potential of public feedback in making the Government more 
responsive and accountable. The Public Affairs Centre (PAC) in Bangalore, India 
and Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB), in particular, designed 'Report 
Cards on Public Services' in 2000, which proved to be relatively uncomplicated 
and widely replicable tools for improving transparency and public 
accountability. 
* In the chapter titled 'Teacher management and behaviour', the Report opines 
that corrupt practices in teacher management and distortions in teacher behaviour 
can also have a high incidence on educational quality. 
More globally, a variety of misbehaviours as sociated with teachers can disturb 
the implementation of planned interventions within the education sector, and 
particularly progress toward Education for All goals. Any plan to increase access 
to education, improve educational quality or reduce school inequities may thus 
prove unsuccessful if it does not properly take into consideration issues such as 
unauthorized fees for school admission, teacher -student relationship for private 
gain, and embezzlement of school finances. A study demonstrated, for instanc e, 
that a 10 per cent increase in teacher absence is associated with a 1.8 per cent 
decrease in student attendance. At the same time, another study conducted by the 
World Bank showed that teacher absenteeism is not a marginal phenomenon. It 
can be as high as one third of all teachers in the State of Uttar Pradesh, India 
(World Bank, 2004). 
* The chapter also contains a table showing Major sources of unethical behaviour 
among teachers in South Asia. The report deals with 'Teacher absence rate in 
various countr ies and cost implications'. India  has also been included in .the 
table with 25% teacher absence rate in primary schools with consequent budget 
leakage of 22.5%. 
* The analysis conducted by Chaudury et al (2005) in Bangladesh, India, 
Indonesia, Peru and Ugand a, for instance, shows that there is no significant 
relationship between teachers' absenteeism and their residence within the 
catchments area of school, their average tenure in the school and how recently 
they have attended a training programme. 
* In the sub-topic "Designing and enforcing teachers' codes of conduct", the Report 
concludes that Even though codes of conduct are generally perceived as useful 
instruments, they are not always effectively enforced. Various modes of 
enforcement have been experimented  throughout the world, with more or less 
success. Existing social, political, cultural and institutional factors in Bangladesh, 
India  and Nepal have greatly influenced the implementation of these codes. 
* In the chapter -7 which deals with exams; credentials and accreditation, the 
Report mentions that in some places in India,  cheating is now so well 
established that when Universities try to resist, students protest and demand their 
traditional right to cheat. In the Report, some examples of academic fraud have 
been mentioned. One of them is related to the findings of The Commission

of Investigation on Abuse of Authority in Nepal, which suspects that 10% of the 
Himalayan Kingdom's 1,40,000 school teach ers are using diplomas purchased 
from India (Chronicle of Higher Education, 2003). Similarly, some press reports 
on figures on academic fraud have been included, which are as under:- 
lndia: fees for manipulating entrance tests scores between USS 80 and USS  
20,000 for the most popular programmes, such as computer sciences, medicine 
or engineering. 
India: Post dated cheques totaling more than US$300,000 collected by people 
offering to sell answers for a Nationwide examinations for physicians. 
* In the chapter titled 'Private tutoring: How to avoid the corruption of mainstream 
education?', the Report mentions that according to a recent comparative study 
undertaken by the HEP on teachers codes of conduct in South Asia, private 
tuition is thus regarded as a major s ource of unethical behaviour in Bangladesh, 
India and Nepal. 
* The Report also says that in India, a 1997 survey of 7,879 primary schools pupils 
in Delhi found that 39.2 per cent were receiving tutoring. Other reports have 
suggested that 70 per cent of urban children receive private tutoring in one or 
more subjects. 
* In the chapter regarding memo to policy makers, planners and managers on how 
to address the challenge of corruption in the Education Sector, there is a subtopic 
titled 'How to address external fac tors (mainly political, legal, economical and 
educational)'. 
This chapter mentions that lessons from experience and evidence suggest that 
five key elements hold a lot of promise when they can coalesce, namely), 
leadership; competition in the political and economic arena; the right to 
information; collective action; and an integrated approach. 
Under sub-title 'Right to Information' the Report concludes that freedom of the 
press and access to information is key to transparency and accountability. The 
experiences of countries such as India that have progressively provided a legal 
basis for the right to information can prove extremely useful in this regard.

Advanced communication facility for tsunami warning system 
139. MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of EARTH SCIENCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether, in order to speed up India's tsunami warning system, it is proposed to 
set up an advanced communication facility, to enable immediate transfer of information 
from data collection centres along the coastline to a central institute; 

48     Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
(b) if so, the details thereof: and 
(c) by when the new system would start functioning and how far this would help to 
cut the delays in timely relaying of information, to control loss of life and property? 
THE MINISTER OF EARTH SCIENCES (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
Communication of real time data from Tide Gauges and Bottom Pressure Recorders to 
the Early Warning Centre at Indian Natio nal Centre for Ocean Information Services 
(INCOIS), Hyderabad is very critical for generating timely tsunami warning and advanced 
communication facilities are being established. At present real-time data is being received 
at INCOIS through V -SAT connectivi ty from the already installed Tide gauges and 
Bottom Pressure Recorders (BPRs). The Seismic data from the Real Time Seismic 
Monitoring Network being installed by India Meteorological Department (IMD) will be 
received at Central Receiving Station in INCOIS through V-SAT connectivity. The entire 
system is expected to be operational by September 2007. A Virtual Private Network for 
Disaster Management Support (VPNDMS) node has been setup at INCOIS that facilitates 
reliable connectivity to the Ministry of Home Affairs for dissemination of Warnings. 
(c) The tsunami warning system is scheduled to be operational by the end of 
September 2007. Coastal areas will  be identified with respect to their vulnerability to 
various scenarios of tsunamis using tsunami models. Th e warnings will be issued within 
an hour of Tsunami causing Earthquake, while the tsunami alert will be generated within 
half an hour of the Earthquake. This will  give a minimum of two hours to inhabitants in 
the coastal India, except for Andaman & Nicobar  Islands. For the islands, the alert itself 
will be warning.

Storage facility for fruits and vegetables 
141. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: Will the Minister of FOOD PROCESSING INDUSTRIES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a large quantity of fruits and vegetables are wasted in the 
country every year due to shortage of proper storage facility; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c). the steps taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF FOOD PROCESSING 
INDUSTRIES (SHRI SUBODH KANT SAHAY): (a) to (c) According to the Vision 2015 
report prepared by Rabo India Finance Pvt. Ltd., wastage of Agricultural food items 
(including fruits) is estimated to be about Rs. 58,000 crore annually, occurring at various 
stages of handling after harvesting due to lack of adequate post -harvest infrastructure, 
lack of cold chain facilities, transportation, proper storage facilities etc. Wastage of fruits 
and vegetables is estimated to be of the order of 22% due to such inadequate facilities. 
The Government, through its schemes for financial assistance and other promotional 
measures, facilitates creation of food related infrastructure aimed at reducing wastages, 
enhancing value additi on and increasing shelf life. The Ministry of Food Processing 
Industries, through its plan schemes during Xth Plan, has been promoting development' 
of infrastructure for food processing industries including cold storages as integral part of 
processing units or part of common facilities in Food Park. During the Xth Plan, the 
Ministry has implemented a scheme for cold chain facilities whereunder asistance upto 
25% of the cost of plant & machinery and technical civil works in general areas and 
33.33% in diffic ult areas with a common ceiling of Rs. 75 lakhs was admissible to all 
implementing agencies. During the XI Plan, the Ministry is working on launching a 
revamped comprehensive Cold Chain Infrastructure Scheme for creating integrated cold 
chain infrastructur e at different levels -farm level primary processing centre -cum-cold 
chain, collection/aggregation centers and Strategic Distribution Centers. The initiative 
being undertaken by the Ministry are aimed at filling the gaps in the supply chain, 
strengthening o f cold chain infrastructure leading to overall development of food 
processing industries and reduction in wastages.

Effect of expansion of economy on children 
179. SHRI AMIR ALAM KHAN: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 

Written Answers to [13 AUG.. 2007] Unstarred Questions     73 
(a) whether mere expansion of Indian economy will be able to address the issues 
relating to the plight of children who are suffering from under -nourishment, anaemia 
and basic schooling facilities; 
(b) whether it is a fact that Government have failed to provide guarantee to the right 
to education in many parts of the country; and 
(c) if so, the reason therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FA TMI): (a) The National Nutritional 
Policy, 1993 states that "Mere economic development, or even the adequacy of food at 
household levels, are no guarantees for a stable and satisfactory nutritional status. 
However, the overall development strategy of a cou ntry is likely to have a pronounced 
bearing on what nutritional planning can accomplish. ... Nutrition is a multi -sectoral 
issue and needs to be tackled at various levels. Nutrition affects development as much 
as development affects nutrition". 
(b) and (c) The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserts Article 21-A in the 
Constitution which provides that "the State shall provide free and compulsory education 
to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by 
law, determine". Section 1(2) of the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act provides that 
"it shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in 
Official Gazeette, appoint". This notification has not yet been issued pending enactment 
of the consequential legislation envisaged under Article 21-A. A draft Model Right to 
Education Bill,  spelling out broad parameters and features for achieving the 
Constitutional mandate of free and compulsory education was drafted and circulated as 
framework to the States/Union Territories to seek their comments thereon.

revealed that India is facing a deep crisis in higher education, with declining standards

cent of the relevant age group of students go for university education, higher education 
whereas in many developing countries the percentage is between 20 and 25;

Review of strength of judges 
216. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTI A: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there was a need for strengthening the legal aid system, to provide 
access to justice to the people; 
(b) whether taking into consideration the huge backlog of cases, Government are 
contemplating to increase the strength of High Courts and Supreme Court judges and was 
reviewing the situation once in three years, both in the High Courts and Supreme Court; 
(c) if so, whether the strength of judges would be increased; and 
(d) by when a final decision to increase the strength of judges would be taken? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) Yes, Sir. To 
provide for free and competent legal services to the weaker sections of the society to 
ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of 
economic or other disabilities, and to organise Lok Adalats to secure that the operation 
of the legal system promotes justice on - a basis of equal opportunity, the Legal Services 
Authorities Act, 1987 was enacted. Further, Section 12 of the National Legal Services 
Act, 1987 provides for free legal aid to certain categories such as members of SCs & 
STs, victims of trafficking in human beings or beggar, a woman or a child, mentally ill  
or otherwise disabled person etc. irrespective of income criteria and also other persons 
within the income limit prescribed in the said Act. 
(b) to (d) In pursuance of the judgment of the Supreme Court of October 6, 1993 in the 
Supreme Court Advocates on Record & Anrs. Vs. the Union of India, the judge strength of 
the High Courts is reviewed every three years. As per the guidelines, the required strength 
of permanent Judges in a High Court is worked out by dividing the average institution of 
main cases during the last five years by the national average or the average rate of 
disposal of main cases per Judge per year in the High Court, . whichever is higher. 
Similarly, the required strength of additional judges in a High Court is worked out by 
dividing the number of main cases pending over two years by the national average or the 
average rate of disposal of main cases per Judge per year in that High Court, whichever is 
higher. If the disposal per Judge in the concerned High Court is below even the national 
average then instead of increasing the strength, the concerned High Court is required to 
take steps for improvement in the rate of disposal of cases. If the average disposal of 
concerned High Court is above the national average then increase in Judge strength in 
accordingly considered. The strength of Additional Judges is reviewed only if there is an 
increase in the arrears of the pending cases during the last 5 years and the disposal per 
Judge is above the national average. 
As a result of a triennial review in the year 2006, 106 posts of Judges, subject to 
concurrence of the respective State Governments, have' been approved in various High 
Courts as per details given below:  
(i) Allahabad 65   Judges 
(ii) Andhra Pradesh 27   Judges 
(iii) Calcutta 08   Judges

Since the State Governments have to bear the expenditure on the infrastructure and 
the salaries of the Judges of the High Courts and the connected staff, their approval is 
sought before finally approving the posts. Till date, the State of Uttar Pradesh, Madhya 
Pradesh and Karnataka have agreed to bear the expenditure and accordingly, they have 
been intimated that their strength stands revised. The State Government of Andhra

Impact of power projects in the North East on environment 
232. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the power projects in the North East have been framed though the laid 
down procedures without ignoring environmental concerns; and

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) All power projects 
in the country including those in the North Eastern Region are conceived and their 
various parameters finalised only after detailed survey and investigation and necessary 
studies. Environmental concerns are given due consideration through Environment 
Impact Assessment (EIA) studies and Environment Management Plans (EMPs) formulated

Shortcomings of APDRP 
233. SHRI MOTIUR RAHMAN: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there were significant deficiencies in the quality and reliability of power  
supply, which was targeted under Accelerated Power Development and Reforms  
Programme (APDRP); 
(b) whether the number of feeder trippings and duration of outage, as well the 
failure rate of distribution transfo rmers was much higher than permissible in most 
States; 
(c) whether there is lack of improvement in disposal of consumer complaints; and  
(d) the measures taken to check the shortcomings of APDRP? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) The 
Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) was launched in the 
year 2002-03 with the objective of encouraging reforms and of reduction in Aggregate 
Technical and Commercial (AT&C) losses, improving quality of supply of power and  

118   Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
improving consumer satisfaction. The number of feeder trippings and duration of outage 
as well as failure rate of distribution transformers are quite high in many towns. The 
main reasons for these are old and overloaded distribution systems, lack of proper 
maintenance of distribution system, power shortages, no proper MIS etc. 
(c) Section 42 of the Electricity Act 2003 provides for establishment of a forum for 
redressal of grievances of consumers and for the appoin tment of an Ombudsman. 
Further, State Power Utilities have been advised to establish consumer care centres for 
addressing consumer grievances/complaints. Utilities in the States of Andhra Pradesh, 
Delhi, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Hary ana, Himachal Pradesh, 
Goa, Assam, Punjab, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, 
Tripura and West Bengal have established consumer care centers in their select towns.  
(d) The Government took up independent evaluation of APDRP through independent 
agencies, while recommending the continuance of APDRP beyond the Tenth Plan, the 
evaluators made certain suggestions for incorporating in the programme for achieving 
better results, the Utilities and the Planning Commission had also proposed certain 
modifications in the programme. Considering this, the Ministry of Power constituted a 
Task Force, headed by Shri P. Abraham, former Secretary, Government of India, to 
assess and analyze the current efforts, suggestions made by various agencies and to 
suggest restructuring of the programme to achieve the objectives of APDRP. The Task 
Force recommended the following:—  
 
• Eligibility criteria may be made more stringent to push States towards reforms 
• The assistance under the programme should focus mainly on activ ities which 
will help in quick reduction of AT&C loss and improvement in customer 
services. AT&C loss reduction target should be realistic depending on the 
current level of each utility. 
• The focus of the programme may be on following activities. 
o   IT based energy accounting and auditing supported by GIS based o 
consumer indexing 
o Spot billing, computerized billing  and revenue collection 
o Consumers care centers schemes for reducing technical loss 
o Reduction in theft and pilferage 
° Better operation and monitoring of network 
• Quality Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) should be prepared based on verifiable 
data. 
• 10%-15% variation in quantity and price of components may be allowed 
within overall cost of the scheme.

Identification of hydro power potential 
† 240. SHRI JAI PARKASH AGGARWAL: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) the extent to which hydro power potential has been identified in the country as 
on date and the extent to which the same has been tapped; 
(b) whether Government propose to prepare a hydro power policy to fulfil the rising 
demand of power in all the areas; 
†Original notice of the question was received   in Hindi. 

126   Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the target fixed regarding the amount to be spent in the current Plan period to 
raise the power production capacity in the country. 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) As per the re-
assessment studies completed by the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) in 1987, the 
hydro electric potential of the country in terms of installed ca pacity has been estimated 
to be about 1,48,700 MW. Presently, a capacity of 30,951.5 MW (20.81%) has already 
been developed and 14951 MW (10.05%) of capacity is underdevelopment. In addition 
to the above, pumped storage capacity of 3884.6 MW is in operation and pumped 
storage schemes of 1925 MW are under construction. About 69.13% of the identified 
potential is yet to be developed. 
(b) and (c) The policy on hydro power development announced by the Government 
in August, 1998 incorporates several steps and me asures for expeditious development of 
hydro power. It lays emphasis on basin -wise development, evolving consensus on inter -
State issues, mitigation of geological risks, simplified procedure for transfer of 
clearances, promoting joint venture arrangements etc. It also lays emphasis on increasing 
private investment in the power sector through Independent Power Producers (IPPs) and 
joint ventures. The Electricity Act, 2003 has also created a conducive environment for 
investments in all segments of the industry  both for public sector and private sector by 
removing barriers to entry. The Natioanl Electricity Policy (February, 2005) also lays 
emphasis on private sector participation in generation including hydro generation.  
Water including water power being a Stat e subject, some of the State Governments 
also have their own policies on hydro power development. 
(d) During the Eleventh Plan about 16533 MW of power is proposed to be added 
through hydro electric projects at an estimated cost of about Rs. 78100 crores.

241. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether after the dismal performance during the Tenth Five Year Plan, the power 
sector is facing a similar fate during the Eleventh Five Year Plan w ith the Centre, States 
and private companies are estimated to fall short of a massive Rs. 450,000 crores during 
2007 to 2012; 
(b) whether the country needs about Rs. 10,31,600 crore to add more power than 
70,000 MW of generation capacity, besides creating and upgrading transmission and 
distribution systems; and

power shortage during the eleventh Five Year Plan?

Group on Power for the Eleventh Plan (2007 -12) based on certain assumptions, has 
estimated a total fund requirement of about Rs. 10,31,600 crores for the power sector as 
a whole. For creation of projected capacity addition, fund requirement has been 

Written Answers to [13 AUG., 2007] Unstarred Questions    127 
assessed at about Rs. 4,10,900 crores by the Working Group. Out of the now proposed 
capacity addition of about 78500 MW, 1870 MW has already been commissioned and 
another 50,975 MW is under constructi on. Power Finance Corporation and Rural 
Electrification Corporation have geared up to mobilize funds to ensure that viable 
projects do not suffer for want of funds. Further, to facilitate financial closure in respect 
of private sector projects, an Inter In stitutional Group, comprising of leading financial

pleased to refer to answer to Unstarred Que stion 2985. given in the Rajya Sabha on the 
30th April, 2007 and state: 
(a) the estimated quantity of coal and gas required per year for the thermal power 
stations proposed to be set up during the Eleventh Five Year Plan; and 
(b) the arrangement proposed for its supply? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) During the 
terminal year of the Eleventh Plan (2011 -12), the estimated quantity of coal and gas 
required for the thermal power stations (TPSs) now proposed to be set up during the 
Eleventh Plan would be as under: 
i.    Coal Requirement :     262 Million Tonne 
ii.   Average Gas Requirement   :     20 Million Metric Standard Cubic Meter per day 
(b) Coal requirement of the thermal power stations proposed to be set up during the 
Eleventh Plan (except for Trombay TPS, Sikka TPS, Torangallu TPS and part 
requirement of Krishnapatnam TPS which are based on imported coal) would be met 
from Coal India Ltd., Singareni Coalfields Ltd. and captive mines of TPSs, Shortfall, if 
any, is proposed to be met through imported coal. 
The requirement of gas for gas based power plants proposed to be set up during the 
Eleventh Plan is envisaged to be met through indigenous sources, such as ONGC, IOC, 
PMT, JV and import of LNG.

249. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that despite all  the steps taken, the condition of the power in 
the country is not upto the mark: 
(b) if so, the shortage of electricity. State-wise; and 
(c) the action Government propose to take during the Eleventh Five Year Plan? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSH1L KUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) There is 
overall shortage of power in the country. The shortages vary from State to State and 
season to season as well as times of the day depending on demand and supply of power. 
During April-July!. 2007, the energy and peak shortage in the country were 18,969 MU 
(7.9%) & 13,686 MW (13.4%) respectively. The State -wise details of shortage of power 
in the country during July, 2007 and April-July, 2007 are given in the Statement -I and II 
(See below). 
(c) The actions being taken/proposed to be taken by the Government in the Eleventh 
Five Year Plan to bridge the gap between demand and supply of electricity inter alia 
include: 
> Augmentation of generation capacity. Capacity addition to the tune of 78,500 
MW is proposed for the Eleventth Plan. 
>  Development of Ultra Mega Power Projects of 4000 MW capacity each under 
tariff based competitive bidding route. 
> Strengthening of inter -state and inter -regional transmission capacity for 
optimum utilization of available power. 
> Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) for 
reduction of AT&C losses, etc. 
>  Harnessing surplus captive power into the grid. 
> Promoting demand side  management, energy efficiency and energy 
conservation measures.

251.  SHRIMATI HEMAMAL1NI: 
MS. SUSHILATIRIYA:

(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether in view of the above hike Government would ensure that p ower supply 
would be uninterrupted; and 
(d) whether, at present, there is no power supply for hours together in certain areas 
in the capital? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) As per 
the provisions of Electricity Act, 2003, determina tion of tariff to be pharged by the 
distribution licensees is the statutory function of the State Electricity Regulatory 
Commissions (SERCs). The Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission (DERC) has informed 
that its Multi Year Tariff (MYT) Regulations for t he period 2007 to 2011 have already 
been notified by the Government of NCT of Delhi on 30th May, 2007. For deciding the 
tariff orders for 2007-08, the DERC has given in the Licensees 90 days time to file their 
Petitions under the MYT regime. Meanwhile, BSE S Rajdhani Power Ltd. (BRPL) and 
BSES Yamuna Power Ltd. (BYPL) have filed Petitions before DERC for a hike in tariffs 
on the ground that the Tariff Orders under the -MYT regime for 2007- 08 may be issued 
as late as November, 2007 and they are facing high pow er purchase cost. Till such time 
the DERC takes a view on the Petitions for interim hike or on the Petitions yet to be 
filed by the Distribution Companies under the MYT regime, the exsisting tariff structure 
in the NCT of Delhi shall continue. 
(c) and (d) Section 86(l)(i)  of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides that the State 
Commission shall specify or enforce standards with respect to quality, continuity and 
reliability of service by licensees. The DERC has informed that the Government of NCT 
of Delhi has a lready constituted a 'Delhi Power Procurement Group' for buying power 
for Delhi; the Group has entered into Power Purchase Agreements even at the high rates 
ranging from Rs. 5 to Rs. 7 per unit so as to ensure uninterrupted power supply to the 
citizens of Delhi. Furthermore, in case of short supply, load shedding takes place first in 
those areas where Aggregate Technical and Commercial Losses (AT&C) are high.

Tribal development proposals of Andhra Pradesh 
270. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Will the Minister of TRIBAL AFFAIRS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) the details of the latest status of the proposals for tribal development received 
from Government of Andhra Pradesh which are still  pending for approval; 
(b) the reasons for delay in clearing these proposals; 
(c) by when these proposals are likely to be cleared; and 
(d) the details of the ongoing tribal development projects in the State along with 
those proposed to be implemented during the current year and the next? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI PR. KYNDIAH): (a) to (d) Ministry  
of Tribal Affairs provides financial assistance to State Governments for the welfare of 
Scheduled Tribes under various schemes/programmes of the Ministry based on the 
allocation criteria prescribed under the guidelines. Funds are released subject to fulfillment 
of prescribed conditions which inter alia includes submission of utilization certificates* 
for the fund released in previous years, the details of proposals received from the 
Government of Andhra Pradesh during 2007-08 are as under: 
(i) Release of R s. 600 lakh to Girijan Cooperative Corporation Ltd. (GCC), 
Visakhapatnam under the scheme of Grant-in-Aid to STDCCs etc. for Minor 
Forest Produce (MFP) Operations: 
(ii) Proposals under Article 275 (1)  of the Constitution for an amount of Rs. 
2599.76 lakh from Government of India. 
The aforesaid proposals are processed as per prescribed procedure under the 
respective scheme/programme and funds and the timing of release is subject to fulfilment 
of prescribed conditions. In case of 'Grant -in-Aid to STDCCs etc. for Minor Forest 
Produce (MFP) Operations', the scheme is under review in the light Of the instructions/ 
guidelines for continuation of the existing schemes during Eleventh Plan. 
The State Government and Intergrated Tribal Development Agencies (ITDAs) 
implement a number of tribal development projects/ scheme in tribal areas for the welfare/ 
development of the Scheduled Tribes under Tribal Sub Plan (TSP) and details of such 
tribal development projects are not maintained in this Ministry. 
New Anganwadi Centres 
271. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether 14 lakh Anganwadi Centres (AWCs) were to be sanctioned by December, 
2008 and if so, whether only 10.53 lakh AWCs were sanctioned till 31st March, 2007; 
(b) whether more than 2.72 lakhs of AWCs already sanctioned are not operational 
till date; if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether the Apex Court has directed Government to operationalise the balance 
of sanctioned AWCs by 15th July. 2007; and 
(d) if so, the steps being taken to comply with the directives of the Apex Court?  

160   Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. As per the 
Hon'ble Supreme Court's directions of 13.12.2006, minimum of 14 lakh Anganwadi Centres 
(AWCs) are to be sanctioned and operationalized in a phased manner by December. 
2008. It takes about one year from the date of sanction, for an Anganwadi Centre (AWC) 
to become operational. As on 31.03.2007, out of 10.53 lakh sanctioned AWCs, 8 45 lakh 
AWCs are fully functional. The reasons for the backlog are State specific and include 
delays in appointment of AWW's and AWH's, court cases etc. 
(c) and (d) The Supreme Cou rt in its Order of 9th July, 2007 directed all the States 
to operationalize the AWCs sanctioned upto September, 2006, by 15th July, 2007 with 
the exception of the State of Uttar Pradesh, who were directed to operationalize the 
AWCs by 31st July, 2007. 
Following the directions, the States/UTs were addressed on 10.7.2007 to strictly 
adhere to the time-frame laid down by the Apex Court. 
Guidelines to protect rights of Children 
272. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA:. Will the Minister of WOMEN AND  
CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the National Human Rights Commission has come out with detailed 
guidelines to protect and promote the rights of children following the killing  of children 
in Nithari and constituted a five member committee to formulate guidelin es to deal with 
the cases of missing children in an effective and meaningful manner; 
(b) whether the committee has already submitted its report; • 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) the recommendations thereof; and 
(e) by when the recommendations are likely  to be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. 
(c) and (d) A copy of the gist of the report alongwith recommendations is available 
at the website of the National Human Rights Commission at www.nhrc.nic.in. 
(e) The recommendations of the Report relate to several Ministries which are 
individually taking appropriate action. Ministry of Women and Child Development is 
implementing the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2000 for protection 
of children in need of care and protection and children in conflict with law. The Ministry 
is also implementing a programme for Juvenile Justice for establishment, upgradation 
and maintenance of various levels of institutions for juveniles. Child Line, a 24 hour 
emergency phone service is available for children in need of care and protection in 
emergency situations. In addition, the Ministry is also implementing a Scheme for 
welfare of working chi ldren in need of care and protection to provide non -formal 
education and vocational training. 
Rehabilitation of children 
273. SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD  
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 

Written Answers to [13 AUG.. 2007] Unstarred Questions    161 
(a) whether her Ministry has urged the Chief Ministers of all  the States seeking a 
follow-up report on the measures taken for rehabilitation of the children affected by the 
Ministry of Labour's ban on employment of children, issued in October, 2006; 
(b) if so, whether enforcement of the ban has laid  off a large number of children who 
now require rehabilitation and assistance, especially in big cities: 
(c) whether the State Governments have already submitted the lists to Government, 
and 
(d) whether her Ministry is satisfied with the rehabilitation plan being implemented 
in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (d) Government of India held consultations with the State Governments, Non-
Governmental Organizations and other stakeholders at various zonal conferences during 
which the action plans of the State Governments were discussed for effective 
implementation of the Notification and for rehabilitation of affe cted children. Ministry 
of Labour and Employment is implementing the National Child Labour Project [NCLP] 
in 250 districts of 20 States in the country under which children withdrawn from work 
are provided education, nutrition, vocational training, stipend and health care etc., and 
are finally mainstreamed to regular education system thus providing for their over all 
rehabilitation. 
Ministry of Women and Child Development is implementing a Scheme for Working 
Children in Need of Care and Protection under which working children are provided non 
formal eduation, vocational training, to working children to facilitate their entry/re -entry 
into mainstream education in cases where they have either not attended any learning 
system or where their education has been di scontinued, with a view to preventing their 
continued future exploitation.

278. SHRIMATI N.P DURGA: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD

constituted by the Registration Committee, under the Insecticides Act, 1968. The 
recommendations of the Expert Group regarding twenty one pesticides have been 
accepted by the Government. Consequently, the use of Fenitrothion and Fenthion is 
banned in agriculture except for locust control in scheduled desert area and public 
health and the use of Diazinon has been banned in agriculture except for household 
purposes. The use of Metoxuron has also been withdrawn. The recommendations 
regarding remaining pesticides are under consideration of the Government. 
(c) The Government does not have any report regarding sale of banned pesticides.  
(d) Does not arise. 
(e) The Insecticides Act, 1968, is already in place which lays down a comprehensive 
policy to prevent the adverse effects of insecticides. The Act regulates the import, 
manufacture, sale, transport, distribution and use of insecticides with a view to preventing 
risk to human be ings or animals, and for matters connected therewith. The Act, inter 
alia, provides for penal action against, manufacture, sale and distribution of spurious 
pesticides. Promotion of Integrated Pest Management, a strategy which envisages 
cultural, mechanical and biological methods of pest control and need based judicious 
use of pesticides, is also an important constituent of the Government policy. The Central 
and State Governments also take steps to create awareness among the farmers for safe 
use of pesticides.

Patenting of Indigenous Seeds by Multinational Companies 
†*9. SHRI SURENDRA LATH: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that some of the multinational companies are misleading the 
poor farmers by patenting indigenous seeds in the name of GM (Genetically Modified);  
(b) if so, the action taken by Government a gainst such companies and the efforts 
made to check it; and 
(c) the effort being made by Government for scientific study and development of the 
indigenous seeds? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) and (b) Bt. 
cotton is the only genetically mo dified crop approved for commercial cultivation in the 
country by Genetic Engineering Approval Committee of the Ministry of Environment and 
Forests constituted under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. All the Bt. cotton 
hybrids have been developed by private seed companies from Indian cultivators using 
genetically modified seeds procured from Monsanto of USA, Biotechnology Transgenes 
China Corporation and UT, Kharagpur. Seeds are not patentable under Section 3 (j) of 
The Patents Act, 1970 as amended in  2002. However, the Protection of -Plant Varieties 
and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001 has been enacted and operationalized for protection of the 
rights of farmers, plant breeders, researchers and local communities. 
(c) Indian Council of Agricultural Research has sanctioned a project for development 
of Transgenics to increase yield and quality of different crops. The National Agriculture 
Research System is continuously engaged in development of new and improved varieties 
of crops.

* 10. SHRI K.E. ISMAIL: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE to 
pleased to state:

Chikungunya in Kerala in large scale, affecting thousands of people and resulting in the 
death of a number of people;

(c) whether a Central team consisting of scientists and experts was sent to the State 
to assess the situation; 
(d) if so, the details and findings thereof; and 
(e) the details of the assistance extended by the Central Government to the State 
Government to fight the disease? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAM-
DOSS): (a) to (e) Chikungunya fever was reported first time in Kerala during 2006 with 
a total 70731 suspected cases and no death. Out of the total 235 samples tested, 43 
(18.29%) were confirmed serologically for Chikungunya. In the year 2007, there were 
21590 suspected Chikungunya fever cases. However, no death has been reported till 5th 
August. Out of the 3845 samples tested, 550 (14.30%) have been confirmed 
serologically for Chikungunya. 
Central Teams comprising officers from the Ministry, Directorate Gen era! of Health 
Services, National Institute of Communicable Diseases (NICD), National Vector Borne 
Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP), Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) 
and experts from National Institute of Virology (NIV), Pune visited Kerala during 28th 
May - 1st June, 10- 13 June, and 14- 18  July, 2007. The gist of the observations made 
by the teams is under: 
1. Comparatively Chikungunya fever cases are less in 2007 than in 2006. However, 
the transmission of Chikungunya is still continuing. 
2. The epidemiological, clinical, entomological and lab investigations confirmed 
that many districts of Kerala are in the grip of Chikungunya fever outbreak. 
3. Patients admitted in hospitals need to be protected from mosquito bite to 
prevent spreading of infection. 
4. IEC activity needs to be strengthened. 
5. The comprehensive medical audit of all  deaths, which has been initiated in 
the State, must continue before a death is considered due to Chikungunya. 
6. Media sensitization on daily  basis is required by authorized officials. 
7. Daily activity chart for prevention and control activities is required and 
should be monitored. 
8. High level Central Team also visited and examined the reported case of 
tomato fever and found that this was due to chickenpox. In any of the 
suspected Chikungunya patient, no unusual skin manifestation was noticed. 
Director General, ICMR, informed that the Chikungunya virus isolated from 
samples collected from Kerala has been indentified as the same that caused 
outbreaks in neighbouring States of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu currently 
and also in Kerala last year. 
In addition to supply of regular logistics (Adulticides and larvicides), an amount of 
Rs. 220.50 lakh was released to the State during 2006- 07, as emergency package for 
prevention and control activities of Chikungunya. During 2007 -08 also, Rs. 403.90 lakh 
has been released.

Conversion of fertile land into industrial area 
*14. DR. E.M. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether his Ministry is aware of the conversion of fertile land into industrial area 
leading to migration and decrease of agricultural production in rural area; and 
(b) if so, what are the steps taken by inter-Ministerial meeting to regulate the same? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) and (b) As per 
available estimates, there is a marginal decline in cultivable land from 185.09 million ha. 
in 1980-81 to 183.10 million ha. in 2004- 05 due to increase in population and diversion 
of agricultural land for non- agricultural purposes such as urbanization, roads, industries, 
etc. Though there has been a marginal decline in the cultivable land in 2004 -05 as 
compared to 1980-81, the net sown area has more or less remained the same or slightly 
increased by 1.06 million ha. during this period which mainly contribute to the food 
grain production. 
Since the Special Economic Zones (SEZ)  Act, 2005 and SEZ Rules, 2006 came into 
effect on 10th February, 2006, formal approval has been granted for setting up of 362 
SEZs. It may be pointed out that in these 362 formal approvals, the total land area 
involved is only about 48,700 ha. Of these, 90 approvals are in respect of State 
Industrial Development Corporations/State Government Agencies involving land area 
of about 21,400 ha. 
The Government of India constituted an Empowered Group of Ministers (EGOM) to 
consider the issues relating to SEZs and  the EGOM at its meeting held on 5th April, 
2007 recommended that: 

184   Written answers to Starred   [RAJYA SABHA]   Questions for 10th Aug., 2007 
• In respect of pending applications for SEZs, these may be processed for in -
principle, formal approval and, notifications subject to the conditions that the 
state government would not undertake any compulsory acquisition of land for 
such SEZs. 
• Upper limit of the area required for multi product SEZs to be fixed at 5000 
ha. However, State Governments may prescribe a lower limit. 
• A comprehensive Resettlement and Rehabilitation Policy be worked out 
ensuring livelihood from the project to at least one person from each displaced 
family. 
Based on the above recommendations. Government of India has decided that Board 
of Approval (BoA) will not approve any SEZ where the State Govenments have carried 
out or propose to carry out compulsory acquisition of land for such SEZs after 5th April 
2007. However, cases in which all  persons interested in the land either have not 
submitted any objection under Section- 5A or have withdrawn the objections submitted 
and have thus acquiesced in the proposed acquisiution of land may be considered. In 
other cases, where there are objections under Section -5A, the Collector/Acquiring 
Authority may not proceed with the acquisition for the purpose of SEZ and such cases, 
if any, brought before the Board of Approval may not be considered. 
Government of India also constituted another Empowered Group of Ministers to 
consider amendments to the Land Acquis tion Act and Resettlement and Rehabilitation 
policy.

2. SHRI MOTIUR RAHMAN: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to

to the farmers; 
(b) whether the report of the National Sample Survey Orga nization (NSSO) has  
revealed that almost 71 per cent of farmers had not even heard of the concept of  
Minimum Support Price (MSP) and almost 81 per cent of farmers were effectively  
unaware of how to use the MSP; and 
(c) if so, the steps taken to generate awareness about MSP operations amongst fanners? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MFNISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL 
BHURIA): (a) Minimum Support Price (MSP) is in the nature of a minimum guaranteed 
price for the farmers offered by the Government for their pr oduce in case the market 
prices fall below that level. If the market offers higher price than MSP, the farmers are 
free to sell at that price. The Government announces MSP for specified agricultural 
commodities on the basis of recommendation of Commission for Agricultural Costs & 
Prices (CACP), the views of the State Governments and Central Ministries as well as 
such other factors considered important for fixation of support prices. The CACP, while 
formulating its recommendations on price policy considers i mportant factors like cost of 
production, changes in input prices, productivity of different crops across States, 
demand supply situation, domestic and international price trends, terms of trade between 
agriculture and non -agriculture sectors, need for cro p diversification, resource use 
efficiency and food security.

Bird flu 
3. SHRI A. VIJYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the competent authority has taken control measures regarding the outbreak 
of H5NI avian influenza outbreak in the north eastern region during the last two months; 
(b) if so the de tails including the source of outbreak, birds culled and the financial 
support provided to the poultry farmers/other citizens as on today, category-wise. State-
wise; and 
(c) if so the details of H5NI avian influenza outbreak in various States including the 
number of birds culled, financial support provided, source of outbreak, total loss due to 
the outbreak, steps taken to control/prevent further outbreak for the last three years, State-
wise, year-wise and category-wise? 
THE M INISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
TASLIMUDDIN): (a) Yes Sir. Only one outbreak of avian influenza (H5N1) has been 
notified in one small unit at Village Chingmeirong of East Imphal District on 25th July 
2007 Control and containment measu res were initiated immediately to stamp out and 
prevent the spread of the disease of poultry. The details are given in the Statement (See 
below). 
(b) A committee has been set up to assess the source of infection in the outbreak  
of avian influenza in Manipur. 
More than 3.36 lakhs poultry have been culled during the control operation in Manipur. 
Compensation is payable for poultry culled in operations and for destruction of feed 
and feed materials. More than Rs. 70.00 lakhs has already been paid as compensati on in 
Manipur. The cost of such compensation is shared by the Government of India on a 
50:50 basis. 
(c) No outbreak from any other State of the North Eastern Region has been reported  
in the last three years. 
Statement 
Measures taken to prevent the spread of the diseases The following 
measures were taken in Manipur to prevent the spread of avian influenza: 
1  Demarcation of infected and surveillance areas was carried out in accordance 
with the Action Plan. An area of 0 -5 kms. was designated as the Infected Z one 
and a further area of 5-10 kms. was designated as the Surveillance Zone. 

198   Written answers to Unstarred [RAJYA SABHA] Questions for 10th Aug., 2007 
2. The poultry, both backyard and commercial, has been culled in a radius of 0 -5 
kms around the affected farm premises. More than 3.36 lakh birds have been killed 
in the control operations. 
3. Other infected materials such as poultry eggs, feathers, feed, feed materials, 
protective cloth used by the staff engaged in operations etc. has also been 
destroyed. Mo re than 25,242 kg of feed material and nearly 28 thousand eggs 
have been destroyed. 
4. Thereafter cleaning and disinfection of the infected premises/area has been 
undertaken, which is under progress. 
5. Physical surveillance in the 5 -10 km area is being continue d to ascertain if there 
is any further unusual mortality. No unusual mortality has been reported in the 
surveillance zone as well as from anywhere else in the State. 
6. The Government of India has maintained strategic reserve of poultry vaccines. 
The option of vaccination is thus available to the country. However, vaccination 
has not yet been introduced in the country. 
7. The personnel involved in containment work were provided personal protective 
equipment and brought under cover of Tamiflu by the health authorities. 
8. It is the policy of the Government of India  to pay compensation to owner for 
culled poultry. The costs are being shared on a 50:50 basis with the State 
Government. More than 70 lakhs Indian Rupees has been paid as compensation.  
Moreover, the following measures have also been taken up by the Government of 
India to prevent spread of the disease to other States: 
1. Action Plan for Preparedness, Control and Containment of Avian Influenza for 
Animal Husbandry has been prepared and circulated by Government of India to 
facilitate action by the State Governments. 
2. Import of poultry & poultry products has been banned completely from Avian 
Influenza positive countries. 
3. All the State Governments have been alerted to be vigilant about the outbreak of 
the disease if any. 
4. Border security formations and custom field formations have been alerted. 
5. State of the north -east specially those bordering outbreak countries like 
Bangladesh. Myanmar and China have been alerted. 
6. Nationwide surveillance is continuing. More than 1,43.00 0 samples have been 
tested at High Security Animal Disease Laboratory (HSADL), Bhopal since 
February 2006. 
7. Testing for Avian Influenza have also been started at Regional Level viz., Regional 
Disease Diagnostic Laboratories, Kolkata, Bangalore, Pune and Jallandhar. So far 
about 37,000 samples have been tested in the regional laboratories. 
8. The training of veterinary personnel in preparedness, control and containment is 
continuing.

9. A National workshop on Preparedness. Control and Containment of Avian 
Influenza was organized at Pune during May 2007 and recently a Regional 
Workshop of the North- Eastern States (Sikkim, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, 
Manipur, Mizoram. Arunachal Pradesh. Nagaland and West Bengal) was organized 
at Kolkata by Government of India from 26-28th July 2007.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL 
BHURIA): (a) The target for production of pulses for 2007- 08 has been fixed 15. 50

through Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR).

proposed to launch "National Food Security Mission" comprising rice, wheat and pulses

BHURIA): (a) and (b) A Statement indicating year -wise and district- wise suicides by

successive monsoon, increasing rural indebtedness, and increase in cost of production/
